The words

Lord, who throughout these forty days
For us didst fast and pray,
Teach us with Thee to mourn our sins
And close by Thee to stay.

As Thou with Satan didst contend,
And didst the vict'ry win,
O give us strength in Thee to fight,
In Thee to conquer sin.

As Thou didst hunger bear, and thirst,
So teach us, gracious Lord,
To die to self, and chiefly live
By Thy most holy Word.

And through these days of penitence,
And through Thy passiontide,
Yea, evermore in life and death,
Jesus, with us abide.

Abide with us, that so, this life
Of suff'ring over past,
An Easter of unending joy
We may attain at last.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (F), on the word “Lord”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

The words are by Claudia Frances Ibotson Hernaman, first published in 1873. The tune, ST. FLAVIAN, is from Day's Psalter, 1563. This version of the melody and the words comes from the Open Hymnal Project.

  • Words (1873): Claudia Frances Ibotson Hernaman (1838–1898)
  • Melody (1563): From Day's Psalter, 1563

Questions about Lord Who Throughout These Forty Days

What is the doh of Lord Who Throughout These Forty Days?

In this version, in F major, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Lord Who Throughout These Forty Days start on?

It starts on d (F in F major), a pickup on the word “Lord” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Lord Who Throughout These Forty Days in the public domain?

Yes. Claudia Frances Ibotson Hernaman died in 1898; the words were first published in 1873 and the music in 1563. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
